Project 58317: Implementation of SB 6

Comments of the Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club in response to
the June 10th letter by Governor Greg Abbott filed in this project

Submitted by: Cyrus Reed, Legislative and Conservation Director, Lone Star
Chapter of the Sierra Club, cyrus.reed@sierraclub.org

July 2nd, 2026


The Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club appreciates the opportunity to file informal
comments related to the letter by Governor Greg Abbott related to data centers and
efforts to assure that costs and other issues do not impact residential electric
consumers and Texans in general. While we recognize that the letter of Governor
Abbott is a directive to the PUCT (as well as providing some recommendations for
legislative action), we advocated for filing the letter in a project so that other
stakeholders and Texans could provide any feedback on the letter and its directive.
While the Sierra Club does not necessarily agree with all of the issues raised in the
Governor’s letter and believe that other important issues like county authority and air
pollution from large computational loads also must be addressed, we do agree that
assuring that residential rates do not increase - and even are reduced - is a goal we as
an organization are in agreement with the spirit of the letter and directive.

It is in this spirit we file these brief, informal comments.

First we recognize that as part of SB 6, there are five separate rulemakings - three of
them ongoing and two finalized - and we have been participating in those rulemakings
and will continue to do so. Still, two of those rulemaking, related to transmission cost
allocation in Project 58000 - and large-load interconnection standards - in Project 58481
- are directly related to the directive of the governor to, in his words “guarantee any data


                                                                                           1
 center development does not come at the cost of Texans and our local communities.”
The Governor, in his letter, directs:

• The Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUC) to take action to ensure that data
centers' interconnections will result in reduced residential electrical bills; and
• The PUC to take action to require data centers to pay for all of their electric
infrastructure costs to ensure that no residential ratepayer is burdened by those costs;
and
• The PUC and ERCOT to review their existing authorities and to identify necessary
actions that can be taken under those authorities to safeguard Texans, their property,
and resources.

Key issues in 58000

The Sierra Club is very supportive of the need to change the current 15-minute 4 CP
method. We are aware of an initial proposal from PUCT staff to change to a 30-minute
12 CP method, and require a minimum demand charge for large loads. While we
believe these are an improvement and would better protect residential ratepayers, we
think the PUCT should look at additional issues, including overall energy use, a
one-hour 12 CP - or even as OPUC has suggested a 52 or 365 CP - and better
identification of specific transmission projects that are only serving large loads and
therefore should be completely be paid for by such large loads. At the same time, as a
state we should avoid overly complex formulas that have led to significant delay in
transmission buildout that would impact our well-functioning energy system.

Key Issues in 58481

The PUCT is still assessing multiple rounds of comments and has not finalized the
rulemaking in 58481, although the closely related PGRR 145 (batch zero study process)
has been adopted. Still, there are important decisions still be be made that could better
protect residential consumers, including:

   ●​ Assuring that all interconnection costs are identified and paid for by the large
      load;
   ●​ Whether $50,000 per MW is the right amount, or should be increased. The Sierra
      Club has advocated for a sliding scale based on the size of the load such that
      larger loads would pay a higher fee per MW;
   ●​ How much of the fee is reimbursed once the large computational load is
      operating, and when the fee is reimbursed. We have advocated that assuming
      that a large load does pay for its total cost, that up to 80 percent of the upfront



                                                                                           2
        fee could be reimbursed after four years, but a part of the fee be retained and
       applied to reduce residential bills which is a way to meet the Governor’s directive.

Separately, we have also advocated that even “smaller” large loads between 25 MWs
and 75 MWs also have similar interconnection standards apply to them since ERCOT
has estimated that up to 14,000 MWs of these “medium” loads are also interested in
coming into our grid. Ignoring these loads - which can also impact residential rates - is
an important consideration.

Other issue that could be addressed by PUCT as allowed by rules and statutes

To assure that all large computational loads be required to pay separately for 100 percent of
the costs necessary to service them, including transmission and energy use, distribution and
financing costs, all private electric utilities, cooperative and municipal utilities should develop a
specific large load tariff schedule, which is the official pricing structure set by utility companies,
including rates based on energy consumption, demand charges and other charges (such as
service fees). Large-load customers must be subject to a tariff schedule that is equal or
proportional to the costs of serving them, mitigating the risk that other classes of retail
consumers are paying unwarranted costs. This may include instituting a new tariff schedule or
amending an existing tariff schedule. As a first step, the PUCT and OPUC could survey existing
utilities - public and private - and REPs to determine if utilities are already assuring there is no
cross-subsidation in the rates paid by large computational loads.

Utilities can also set rate surcharges for capital improvements such as the capacity expansions
and other work often needed to serve large new industrial customers, but those costs are
distributed among all ratepayers. We recommend updating rules to ensure current ratepayers
are not asked to foot the bill when data centers and other large new facilities come to town.

We recognize that the PUCT has more limited authority over rates related to electric
cooperatives and municipal utilities, but as a first step a survey could help. Ultimately, it may
require legislative direction to assure that a separate rate tariff and surcharges are established
everywhere in the state, but a survey would be a good first step.


Energy and Water Use Reporting

We are strong advocates for requiring large computational loads to report on their
annual water and energy use, and agree with the further directive by the Govenor. We
recognize that depending on existing authority, there may be the need for legislative



                                                                                                     3
 action but do believe that the PUCT has some authority in this area even without
legislation.

Annual Reporting. To accurately understand the impact of any energy and water user and
ensure our state’s long-term water and energy supply remains secure, we need detailed
information about how much water and energy is being used. The lack of transparency and use
of non-disclosure agreements in data center development prevents a clear understanding of
their energy and water consumption and hampers water and energy supply planning at the
state and local levels. Effective planning guides strategic investment and supports smart growth
in Texas. This all relies on good and accurate data. We recommend requiring data centers to
report annually to the PUC on energy use, peak and overall, energy sources used, cooling
systems used, total water consumption (peak water use and total water use), and water
sources, including the amount diverted, to enable a fair assessment of their energy and water
use and impacts on local water and energy resources. The PUC should share this data with
ERCOT and TWDB to be used in the regional and state water planning process, as well as with
TCEQ for their regulatory functions. Reporting could also include information on any backup
power technology utilized. We strongly suggest that these requirements be placed on any
transmission-level large load customer of 25 MWs or greater.

State Public Website: Require PUCT to design, implement, and maintain a publicly accessible
website to provide information about all data centers and other large electric facilities in the
state, including water and energy use.

Bring your Own Power/Capacity: Maybe, but with some caveats

SB 6, approved by the legislature, does not specifically require large loads to bring their own
power plants to be able to interconnect to the grid, though it does require any large load that
wants to co-locate with an existing power plant. In addition, PGGR 145 does provide some
consideration for those bringing their own power to be considered as part of the batch zero
process.

However, the Sierra Club is concerned that a requirement for large computational loads to bring
their own power plant could lead to increases in air pollution, health care costs and local
community impacts. As a state, Texas already has major areas that do not meet federal Clean Air
Act ozone and particulate matter standards, and location of new gas-powered plants in or near
these non-attainment areas could exacerbate the issue for hundreds of thousands of Texans. In
addition, many data centers also have back-up generation - often dirtier diesel-fueled back-up
generation, and we need real reform of permitting and use of these facilities. The Sierra Club
has separate recommendations about how to improve regulation of back-up generation through



                                                                                                   4
 actions by the TCEQ or legislature that are outside the bounds of PUCT authority, but we believe
that any call for bringing more capacity must be balanced against real air quality concerns.

However, capacity does not just mean power plants. It can also refer to increased transmission
capability or even “distributed capacity” such as onsite battery and solar programs, energy
efficiency and weatherization programs, and demand response programs. We believe that data
centers could help our grid by specifically helping to fund and contribute to such programs.
Indeed if we want data centers to lead to reduced costs for residential and other commercial
electric consumers, than creating a system either through a mitigation fee or direct support for
such consumer-friendly solutions could help our grid and reduce residential rates.

While we are unsure of the PUCT’s statutory authority to require investment in such
“distribution” capacity, we believe it is worth considering, and the Sierra Club has already been
suggesting such an approach to the legislature. Assuring that data centers and other large loads
bring real solutions to our water and energy needs by investing in communities could help
mitigate their real impacts.

The Sierra Club appreciates the opportunity to file these brief informal comments.
